# Lab: QoS is checked twice

A ROS 2 publisher and subscription agree on QoS when they meet, at run time,
and a mismatch shows up as messages that never arrive. On a microcontroller
there is no one watching at run time, so nano-ros checks the agreement
earlier, and twice: when the image is built, against the other nodes of the
system, and when the image boots, against what your code asked for. In this
lab you break each check on purpose, read what it says, and then make the
two nodes of chapter 3 agree on a non-default QoS: the talker keeps its last
message for a subscriber that joins late (`transient_local` durability), and
the listener asks for it.

At the end, `nros run` prints `I heard:` again, from a pair that agrees on
`transient_local` in its code and in its contract.

The lab starts from the workspace of chapter 3: `sensor_node` publishes on
`/chatter` and `monitor_node` subscribes to it. Run every step from the root
of `sensor_ws`, in a shell where ROS 2 is sourced. It takes about an hour,
most of it reading.

## What `transient_local` buys, and costs

A `volatile` publisher sends each message to the subscribers that exist when
it publishes, and forgets it. A subscriber that starts a second later has
missed it for good. A `transient_local` publisher keeps its last messages and
hands them to a subscriber that joins later, which is what a topic that
changes rarely needs: a map, a configuration, a robot's mode. A node that
boots late, or restarts, still learns the current value without waiting for
the next change.

On a workstation the kept messages live in a heap the middleware grows as it
likes. On a microcontroller every kept message is a buffer fixed when the
image is built, so the build must know which publishers keep messages and how
many. That is why the choice belongs in the contract as well as in the code:
the contract is what the build sizes from, and the code is what runs.

## The contract the scaffold wrote

The bringup holds a contract beside `system.toml`. The scaffold wrote the
talker's row when it made the workspace, and `nros new --to` added the
listener's in chapter 3:

```bash probe=2010 track=installed variant=qemu
cat src/sensor_node_bringup/system.contract.yaml
```

The part that matters (comments trimmed):

```yaml
nodes:
  sensor_node:
    params: {}
    paths:
      on_tick:
        trigger: { timer: { rate_hz: 1 } }
        output: [chatter]
    pub:
      chatter:
        qos:
          durability: volatile
  monitor_node:
    params: {}
    sub:
      chatter:
        qos:
          durability: volatile
```

A contract row states what a node creates and with which QoS. The build
sizes the image from it ([chapter 8](tell-the-build.md) shows how much that
saves), and, which is this lab's subject, checks it. Both rows say `volatile`, which is what the scaffolded code
asks for, so the two checks have nothing to say yet. Every node has a
`params:` line, even an empty one: the build sizes the parameter store from
every node's declaration or from none, and a contract that states some nodes
and not others is refused.

## Check one: the build compares the nodes

Change `monitor_node`'s row to ask for more than the talker offers: a
`transient_local` subscription, against a `volatile` publisher. Replace the
contract with:

```bash probe=2020 track=installed variant=qemu
cat > src/sensor_node_bringup/system.contract.yaml <<'EOF'
version: 1

nodes:
  sensor_node:
    params: {}
    paths:
      on_tick:
        trigger: { timer: { rate_hz: 1 } }
        output: [chatter]
    pub:
      chatter:
        qos:
          durability: volatile

  monitor_node:
    params: {}
    sub:
      chatter:
        qos:
          durability: transient_local

topics:
  /chatter:
    type: std_msgs/msg/String
    pub: [sensor_node/chatter]
    sub: [monitor_node/chatter]
    # Read outside this workspace, by `ros2 topic echo` or a ROS 2 node.
    external: sub
EOF
```

`params: {}` says the node declares no parameters. A C or C++ bringup needs
the key on every row or on none, so write it on both.

Build:

```bash probe=2030 track=installed variant=qemu
nros build 2>&1 | tee build/qos-check-one.log || true
grep 'qos-match' build/qos-check-one.log
```

The `tee` keeps the output in a file, so the `grep` can show the line that
matters. The build stops before it compiles anything:

```text
error: [qos-match] error: incompatible QoS on topic '/chatter' field 'durability': pub '/sensor_node/chatter' offers 'volatile', sub '/monitor_node/chatter' requests 'transient_local' (at topics./chatter.qos.durability)
Error: refusing to emit a SystemModel: 2 contract error(s) (run `check` on the same launch file for source excerpts)
```

This is the rule ROS 2 applies when the two endpoints meet, "requested
versus offered": a subscription may ask for less than the publisher offers,
never more. A `transient_local` subscription wants the samples published
before it joined, and a `volatile` publisher keeps none. ROS 2 would connect
nothing and report an incompatible-QoS event at run time, if anyone listened
for it. Here both rows are in one file, so the build compares them first and
names the topic, the field and both endpoints.

## Check two: the boot compares the contract with the code

Make the talker offer what the listener asks for, in the contract only.
Change the publisher's row:

```bash probe=2040 track=installed variant=qemu
sed -i 's/durability: volatile/durability: transient_local/' \
    src/sensor_node_bringup/system.contract.yaml
```

The two rows agree now, and the build accepts them. Run it:

```bash probe=2050 track=installed variant=qemu
nros run --expect 'I heard:' --timeout 300 2>&1 | tee build/qos-check-two.log || true
grep 'declared QoS' build/qos-check-two.log
grep 'would widen what the code narrowed' build/qos-check-two.log
```

The image builds and boots, then stops. Its console (a C project's, trimmed;
the Rust one prints the same lines with a timestamp):

```text
[WARN] nros: declared QoS: taking durability transient_local on publisher `/chatter`; the call site asked volatile. Change the contract row to keep the call site's.
[ERROR] nros: declared QoS: subscription `/chatter` registers volatile and the contract declares durability transient_local; taking it would widen what the code narrowed. Fix the contract row or the call site.
nros run: the target exited with code 1 after 2.5 s without `I heard:`
```

When a node creates an endpoint, nano-ros compares the QoS the code passed
with the contract's row for it, and the two lines are the two directions of
that rule:

- **A publisher's row may strengthen the call site.** The code asked for
  `volatile`; keeping one sample for a late subscriber costs the image a
  buffer the build already reserved from the row, and every subscriber the
  publisher served before is still served. So the image takes the row's
  value and warns, naming both.
- **A subscription's row may not widen what the call site narrowed.** The
  code subscribed `volatile`, which is the narrower request; the row claims
  `transient_local`. Taking the row would hand the callback samples published
  before it joined, which the code never asked for and may not handle. So the
  image refuses to create the subscription, and the boot fails with
  `DeclaredQosMismatch`.

The contract describes the code; it does not replace it. Where they
disagree, the safe direction is taken with a warning, and the unsafe one is
refused.

## Make the code say it

Change both call sites to `transient_local`, so the code and the contract
say the same thing.

<!-- tabs -->

#### Rust

The talker creates its publisher in `src/sensor_node/src/lib.rs` with
`create_publisher_for_topic`; the `_with_qos` form takes a `QoSProfile`:

```rust
let pub_chatter = node.create_publisher_for_topic_with_qos::<StringMsg>(
    "/chatter",
    QoSProfile::default().transient_local(),
)?;
```

The listener's `create_subscription_for_callback_name` has no QoS form; the
one that does, `create_subscription_for_topic_with_qos`, names the callback
after the topic, so `on_callback` matches `"/chatter"` instead of
`"on_chatter"`:

```rust
let _sub = node.create_subscription_for_topic_with_qos::<StringMsg>(
    "/chatter",
    QoSProfile::default().transient_local(),
)?;
```

Both files import `QoSProfile` from `nros`. By hand, or:

```bash probe=2060 track=installed variant=qemu
sed -i -e 's#^use nros::{#use nros::{QoSProfile, #' \
    -e 's#create_publisher_for_topic::<StringMsg>("/chatter")#create_publisher_for_topic_with_qos::<StringMsg>("/chatter", QoSProfile::default().transient_local())#' \
    src/sensor_node/src/lib.rs
sed -i -e 's#^use nros::{#use nros::{QoSProfile, #' \
    -e 's#create_subscription_for_callback_name::<StringMsg>("on_chatter", "/chatter")#create_subscription_for_topic_with_qos::<StringMsg>("/chatter", QoSProfile::default().transient_local())#' \
    -e 's#callback.as_str() == "on_chatter"#callback.as_str() == "/chatter"#' \
    src/monitor_node/src/lib.rs
```

#### C

The talker creates its publisher in `src/sensor_node/src/Talker.c` with
`rclc_publisher_init_default`; the `_with_qos` form takes an `rclc_qos_t`.
Start from the default profile and change one field:

```c
rclc_qos_t qos = RCLC_QOS_DEFAULT;
qos.durability = RCLC_QOS_DURABILITY_TRANSIENT_LOCAL;
rcl_ret_t rc = rclc_publisher_init_with_qos(
    &self->pub, node, ROSIDL_GET_MSG_TYPE_SUPPORT(std_msgs, msg, String),
    "/chatter", &qos);
```

The listener's `src/monitor_node/src/Listener.c` does the same with
`rclc_subscription_init_with_qos`. By hand, or:

```bash probe=2060 track=installed variant=qemu
sed -i -e 's#rcl_ret_t rc = rclc_publisher_init_default(#rclc_qos_t qos = RCLC_QOS_DEFAULT;\n    qos.durability = RCLC_QOS_DURABILITY_TRANSIENT_LOCAL;\n    rcl_ret_t rc = rclc_publisher_init_with_qos(#' \
    -e 's#String), "/chatter");#String), "/chatter", \&qos);#' \
    src/sensor_node/src/Talker.c
sed -i -e 's#rcl_ret_t rc = rclc_subscription_init_default(#rclc_qos_t qos = RCLC_QOS_DEFAULT;\n    qos.durability = RCLC_QOS_DURABILITY_TRANSIENT_LOCAL;\n    rcl_ret_t rc = rclc_subscription_init_with_qos(#' \
    -e 's#String), "/chatter");#String), "/chatter", \&qos);#' \
    src/monitor_node/src/Listener.c
```

#### C++

The talker creates its publisher in `src/sensor_node/src/Talker.cpp`, and
the listener binds its subscription in `src/monitor_node/src/Listener.cpp`.
Both take a QoS after the topic name, the way `rclcpp` does:

```cpp
::rclcpp::Result r = node.create_publisher(
    pub_, "/chatter", ::rclcpp::QoS::default_profile().transient_local());
```

```cpp
::rclcpp::bind_subscription<::std_msgs::msg::String, Listener, &Listener::on_msg>(
    node, "/chatter", this, ::rclcpp::QoS::default_profile().transient_local());
```

By hand, or:

```bash probe=2060 track=installed variant=qemu
sed -i 's#node.create_publisher(pub_, "/chatter");#node.create_publisher(pub_, "/chatter", ::rclcpp::QoS::default_profile().transient_local());#' \
    src/sensor_node/src/Talker.cpp
sed -i 's#node, "/chatter", this);#node, "/chatter", this, ::rclcpp::QoS::default_profile().transient_local());#' \
    src/monitor_node/src/Listener.cpp
```

<!-- /tabs -->

## Run the pair

```bash probe=2070 probe-run=900 track=installed variant=qemu
nros run --expect 'I heard:'
```

```text probe-expect=2070 variant=qemu
I heard:
nros run: matched after
```

The image boots, and the listener hears the talker. The console still
carries warnings, of a different kind (trimmed):

```text
[WARN] nros: qos: publisher '/chatter' asked for TRANSIENT_LOCAL KEEP_LAST(10); this image retains 1 sample(s) per transient-local publisher and replays them on a late joiner's query. Granting 1 and advertising it to the graph.
[WARN] nros: qos: subscription '/chatter' asked for KEEP_LAST(10); this image's receive ring holds 4. Granting 4 and advertising it to the graph. Raise NROS_ZENOH_SUBSCRIBER_RING_DEPTH to keep more.
I heard: [Hello World: 1]
```

These are not mismatches between the code and the contract. They are the
image granting less **depth** than the code asked for: `QoSProfile::default()`,
`RCLC_QOS_DEFAULT` and `QoS::default_profile()` all ask for `KEEP_LAST(10)`,
and this image keeps one sample per transient-local publisher and four per
subscription. The image grants what it has, advertises the granted value to
the ROS 2 graph (so `ros2 topic info -v /chatter` shows the truth), and names
the knob that would raise it.

## Change it

Silence the depth warnings by asking for what the image grants. Add
`depth: 1` beside `durability` in both contract rows, and ask for depth 1 at
both call sites: `.keep_last(1)` on the Rust `QoSProfile`, `qos.depth = 1;`
in C, `.keep_last(1)` on the C++ `QoS`. Run again: the `qos:` lines are gone,
and the image reserves one sample per endpoint instead of the default ring.

Then try the other direction of check two: put the talker's contract row back
to `volatile` while its code keeps `transient_local`. The build refuses it
first (check one, since the listener still asks for `transient_local`); make
the listener `volatile` in both places too, and read what the boot says about
a publisher whose row is weaker than its call site.

## If it doesn't work

- **Step one builds instead of refusing:** compare the file with the one
  above. The listener's row must sit under `nodes:` with the name
  `monitor_node`, and `/chatter` under `topics:` must list
  `monitor_node/chatter` in its `sub:`, so the build knows the two rows
  meet on one topic.
- **Step two fails without a `declared QoS` line:** the build itself failed,
  before the image booted. Read the first `error` in its output; a C or C++
  bringup refuses a contract where some rows carry `params:` and others do
  not.
- **The last run prints `declared QoS` errors again:** one call site still
  asks for `volatile`. Each line names the endpoint (`publisher` or
  `subscription`) and its topic.
- **The listener prints nothing in the last run:** in a Rust project,
  `on_callback` still matches `"on_chatter"`. The `_with_qos` subscription
  names its callback after the topic.

## What just happened

You met the two places a nano-ros system's QoS is checked, and the rule each
applies:

| When | Compares | Rule | On a mismatch |
|---|---|---|---|
| build (`qos-match`) | a subscription's row with its publisher's row | the subscription may request no more than the publisher offers | the build refuses and names topic, field and both endpoints |
| boot, publisher | the call site with the row | the row may strengthen the call site, never weaken it | stronger: taken, with a warning; weaker: refused |
| boot, subscription | the call site with the row | the row may not widen what the call site narrowed | refused (`DeclaredQosMismatch`) |
| boot, any endpoint | the asked depth with the image's pools | the image grants what it has | granted and advertised, with a warning naming the knob |

In ROS 2, all of this happens when two endpoints meet on the network, and a
mismatch is a topic that stays silent. nano-ros states the system in one
contract, so the comparison between nodes moves to the build, and the
comparison between the contract and the code happens once, at boot, before
any message flows. What remains at run time is the same "requested versus
offered" check with peers outside the image, such as `ros2 topic echo`.

## Design background

The contract and what the build derives from it follow RFC-0100. The lab
grows the Tutorial's one project, as RFC-0124 D3 lays out.
